summary: This document updates the Protection State Coordination logic for MPLS-TP linear protection from RFC 6378. It adds rules and recommendations for using TLVs, addresses issues raised in an ITU-T liaison statement, and clarifies behavior in a case RFC 6378 did not explain well.

plainLanguage.summary: If a road is blocked, traffic switches to a backup road, and both ends must agree on when. This RFC fixes some gaps in the rules that tell two ends of a network path how to switch together.

subtitle: Corrections and clarifications to how two MPLS-TP nodes coordinate a switch to a backup path.

tldr.problem: RFC 6378 left gaps in its Protection State Coordination (PSC) logic. A node could report the wrong status after a failure, mismatched settings had no defined outcome, two ends could deadlock while recovering, and handling of simultaneous local and remote requests was unclear.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds TLV format and error-handling rules, replaces specific bullets in RFC 6378, defines which end switches mode on a mismatch, and says PSC must re-evaluate all inputs when the highest-priority one goes away.
tldr.outcome: These are corrections to procedures, not changes to the packet format or the protocol design, and the RFC says it adds no backward compatibility issues with RFC 6378. It updates RFC 6378.

facts.label: IANA action
facts.value: Value 0 in the MPLS PSC TLV Registry marked Reserved

today: RFC 7324 is a Proposed Standard from July 2014 and updates RFC 6378. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Update Changes
sections.content:
This document updates the Protection State Coordination (PSC) protocol of RFC 6378, which handles linear protection in MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP). One update gives rules and recommendations for TLVs. Three address issues #2, #7 and #8 from an ITU-T liaison statement on G.8131/Y.1382. Another clarifies a behavior that RFC 6378 did not explain well.

The RFC states that these are not changes to the packet format or to PSC's design, and that they bring no backward compatibility issues with RFC 6378 implementations. It does not update RFC 7271, but affects it because RFC 7271 builds on RFC 6378.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of fixes to an existing rulebook. The rulebook keeps its shape and only a few rules are patched.

sections.title: TLV Format and Message Checks
sections.content:
Each TLV has three fields in network byte order: a two-octet Type, a two-octet Length and a Value. The Length counts the Value in octets and MUST be a multiple of 4, so the Value may contain explicit padding. A whole TLV is the Value length plus 4. The overall TLV Length field of the PSC message holds the total length of all TLVs.

An implementation SHOULD check that earlier fields agree with RFC 6378, that the message length equals the TLV Length plus 12, and that the TLV lengths add up to the TLV Length. A message failing these checks MUST be dropped, and the operator SHOULD be alerted. A well-formed but unknown or unexpected TLV MUST be ignored and the rest of the message processed as if it were absent.
sections.plainLanguage: Each extra note on a message has a label, a size and contents. If the sizes do not add up, throw the message away. If a note is a kind you do not know, skip it and read the rest.

sections.title: Wrong Status After a Failure
sections.content:
Issue #2 shows that a strict reading of RFC 6378 can leave a node sending NR(0,1) even though the protection LSP (P-LSP) has failed. A node should not send No Request when it has a local failure. The fourth bullet of Section 4.3.3.3 of RFC 6378 is replaced by three bullets:

  • After a local or remote Manual Switch, a local Signal Fail on the protection path SHALL make the LER enter local Unavailable state and send SF(0,0).
  • In local Protecting Administrative state due to a local Forced Switch, a local Signal Fail on the protection path SHALL be ignored.
  • In remote Protecting Administrative state due to a remote Forced Switch, such a Signal Fail SHALL keep the LER in that state and make it send SF(0,1).
sections.plainLanguage: If the backup road is broken, a node must not say 'all is fine'. The new rules say what to say in each case.

sections.title: Handling a Capabilities Mismatch
sections.content:
PSC cannot negotiate properties of the protection domain, but it signals two: the Protection Type (PT) and the Revertive (R) bit. RFC 6378 says an operator is notified on a mismatch but not what the end nodes do. This section answers issue #7.

Three protection types exist: bidirectional switching with a permanent bridge (BP), bidirectional switching with a selector bridge (BS) and unidirectional switching with a permanent bridge (UP). The priority is UP > BS > BP. The node sending the lower-priority type MUST switch to the higher one if it supports it. For an R mismatch, the node indicating non-revertive MUST switch to Revertive if supported.

If a node cannot support the required mode, the pair has a permanent mismatch that only an operator can fix, and the implementation SHOULD alert the operator. It SHOULD still allow traffic on the Working LSP while there is no failure. If a trigger such as SF or MS would cause the protection LSP to be used, the node MUST NOT use it to carry traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: If one end wants one way of switching and the other wants a different way, the one with the lower-ranked way changes if it can. If it cannot, the backup road stays closed and a person is told.

sections.title: Fixing the Reversion Deadlock
sections.content:
Issue #8 describes a deadlock. Both nodes can enter Wait-to-Restore (WTR) at once, receive an out-of-date SF-W indication, move into a remotely triggered WTR and wait for the other end to act. Each then sends NR(0,1) when it should be recovering.

The fix adds a bullet to Section 4.3.3.4 of RFC 6378. A node in Protecting Failure state due to a remote SF-W that receives NR(0,1) SHALL begin recovery. If revertive, it enters Wait-to-Restore, starts the WTR timer and sends WTR(0,1). If non-revertive, it enters Do-Not-Revert and sends DNR(0,1).

A related edit changes the penultimate bullet of Section 4.3.3.3 from 'A remote NR(0,0) message' to 'A remote No Request message' being ignored in local Protecting administrative state. A remote NR now triggers the same behavior whatever the FPath and Path values.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people can each wait for the other to go first, forever. The fix says: when you hear 'nothing is wrong on my side', start getting back to normal.

sections.title: Multiple Inputs to PSC Control
sections.content:
PSC Control logic has two inputs: the Local Request logic and the Remote PSC Request. RFC 6378 describes single inputs but not both together. They can be the same request on both ends, written [L(FS), R(FS)], or different ones, such as [L(LO), R(SF-W)]. Both are handled the same way, and the priority order in Section 4.3.2 of RFC 6378 decides which drives the logic, with local winning ties.

The gap is what happens when the winning input goes away. A strict reading of the state machine would send the node to Normal state (N) before it later noticed the remote request. The RFC calls that unreasonable.

It replaces a paragraph of Section 4.3.3 of RFC 6378. When the highest-priority request is removed or replaced, PSC Control logic SHALL immediately re-evaluate all inputs, local and remote, and change state only after doing so. This requires an implementation to store the most recent local and remote inputs.
sections.plainLanguage: If the boss's order is cancelled, you should look at the other orders right away. You should not act like there were none.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says the changes raise no new security concerns. RFC 6941 is the baseline security discussion for MPLS-TP, and PSC falls under it. Section 2.2 also clarifies how to react to malformed or unexpected messages.

For IANA, the value 0 in the 'MPLS PSC TLV Registry' is marked 'Reserved, not to be allocated', with references to RFC 6378 and this document. The RFC notes that this records an action IANA had already taken but RFC 6378 had not recorded.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is risky here. A number that was never to be used is now written down as off limits.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Type value, recorded in the MPLS PSC TLV Registry.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the Value field in octets; a multiple of 4.
